summary: IPv6 Rapid Deployment (6rd) gives customers IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time, and a DHCP option exists to configure the customer edge device. Often that configuration lives in AAA servers instead. This document defines a RADIUS attribute to deliver 6rd configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: A home router needs settings to use the new internet addresses. This lets the provider's account server hand those settings over.

questions: what is the radius ipv6-6rd-configuration attribute
how does a bng get 6rd settings from radius
how many border relay addresses fit in the 6rd attribute
subtitle: A RADIUS attribute that lets an AAA server hand 6rd settings to the gateway that configures home routers.

tldr.problem: 6rd customer devices get their settings through a DHCP option, but in many networks those settings are stored on AAA servers that speak RADIUS to the Broadband Network Gateway (BNG), not DHCP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6930 defines the IPv6-6rd-Configuration RADIUS attribute (type 173). It carries the IPv4 mask length, the 6rd prefix and one or more Border Relay IPv4 addresses from the AAA server to the BNG, which then answers the customer's DHCP request.
tldr.outcome: A BNG can serve per-user 6rd settings kept in the AAA server. If the attribute is missing, the BNG may fall back to a preconfigured default, and without one the tunnel cannot be established.

today: RFC 6930 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the 6rd specification in RFC 5969.

sections.title: Why 6rd Needs a RADIUS Attribute
sections.content:
6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment, defined in RFC 5969) provides IPv6 service through legacy IPv4-only infrastructure, while IPv4 and IPv6 run side by side. A 6rd Customer Edge (CE) device uses the DHCP 6rd option to discover a 6rd Border Relay (BR) and to configure an IPv6 prefix and address.

In many networks, user configuration is kept on Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) servers, which talk to network elements using RADIUS (RFC 2865). In fixed-line broadband, the Broadband Network Gateway (BNG) is the access gateway and is assumed to embed a DHCP server. The 6rd settings sit in the AAA server, while the customer asks over DHCP, so a new RADIUS attribute is needed to carry the information from the AAA server to the BNG.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings live in one place, but the router asks a different helper. This document gives the two helpers a way to pass the settings along.

sections.title: How DHCP and RADIUS Cooperate
sections.content:
The BNG acts as a RADIUS client and as a DHCP server. The 6rd CE MAY send a DHCPDISCOVER whose Parameter Request option (55) asks for the 6rd option. On receiving it, the BNG SHOULD send a RADIUS Access-Request. Its User-Name attribute (1) SHOULD hold the CE's MAC address, and its User-Password attribute (2) SHOULD hold the shared 6rd password preconfigured on the DHCP server. The recommended MAC format is that of Calling-Station-Id in RFC 3580, without the SSID part.

The BNG asks for the IPv6-6rd-Configuration attribute. If the AAA server approves, the Access-Accept MUST carry the attribute, and the BNG SHOULD answer the CE with a DHCPOFFER containing a DHCP 6rd option.

A second scenario decouples authorization from authentication. The CE sends a DHCPREQUEST, and the BNG's Access-Request SHOULD contain Service-Type (6) with the value Authorize Only (17). Under RFC 5080, that request MUST then contain a State attribute obtained from the earlier authentication. In both scenarios, Message-Authenticator (80) SHOULD protect Access-Request and Access-Accept.
sections.plainLanguage: The router asks the front desk for its settings. The front desk phones the account office, gets the answer, and passes it back to the router.

sections.title: Storing, Fallback and Failover
sections.content:
After the first Access-Accept, the BNG SHOULD store the received 6rd parameters locally. When the CE later asks to extend the lifetime of its address, the BNG does not have to send a new Access-Request, and could reuse the stored values in its reply.

If the Access-Accept has no IPv6-6rd-Configuration attribute, the BNG MAY fall back to a preconfigured default 6rd configuration. With no default, or after an Access-Reject, the tunnel cannot be established. If a default exists but the Access-Accept carries a different configuration, the received configuration MUST be used for the session. If the BNG cannot support the received configuration for any reason, the tunnel SHOULD NOT be established.

Following RFC 2131, if the DHCP server contacted at time T1 has not responded by T2, the CE SHOULD enter the REBINDING state and contact any server. A secondary BNG receiving that message MUST send a fresh Access-Request to the AAA server, and MAY include the IPv6-6rd-Configuration attribute in it.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk writes the settings down so it need not call again. If the office has no answer, it can use a default card, but settings from the office win over the default card.

sections.title: The IPv6-6rd-Configuration Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute has Type 173 and a Length of 28 + n*6 octets, where n is the number of BR IPv4 addresses (at least 1). It is built from three suboptions, because RADIUS has no recommended way to group several attributes and the 6rd configuration needs several IPv4 addresses tied to one IPv6 prefix. The design follows RFC 6158 and refers to RFC 6929.

  • SubType 1 (SubLen 6): IPv4MaskLen, the number of high-order bits identical across all CE IPv4 addresses in a 6rd domain. It may be 0 to 32, and a larger value is invalid. It is a 32-bit field because RFC 6158 forbids 8-bit fields.
  • SubType 2 (SubLen 20): a Reserved field (all zero, MUST be zero when sent and MUST be ignored on receipt), 6rdPrefixLen (MUST be 128 or less) and 6rdPrefix, a 16-octet IPv6 address whose bits beyond the prefix length SHOULD be zero.
  • SubType 3 (SubLen 6): one 6rdBRIPv4Address, repeated for each Border Relay. The 255-octet RADIUS limit allows 37 addresses.

Subtypes can appear in any order. Several subtype 3 entries are RECOMMENDED to sit together.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has three boxes: how much of the street address is shared, the provider's special address prefix, and a list of relay stations. The boxes can come in any order.

sections.title: Where the Attribute May Appear
sections.content:
The attribute is normally used in Access-Accept messages. It MAY appear in an Access-Request as a hint, for example when the BNG has a default 6rd configuration. The RADIUS server MAY ignore the hint and assign different parameters. If the AAA server does not recognize the attribute, it MUST ignore it.

The RFC adds a table to the one in RFC 2865: zero or one instance of the attribute may be present in an Access-Request, Access-Accept or Accounting-Request, and none in an Access-Reject or Access-Challenge.

The attribute is usable in RADIUS or Diameter. Since it was allocated from the standard RADIUS type space, Diameter entities need no special handling (RFC 6733).
sections.plainLanguage: The settings normally come back in the answer. The front desk can also suggest some in its question, but the office does not have to agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that the CE and BNG sit inside a provider network, a closed and lower-threat environment, and the same reasoning applies to the BNG-to-AAA exchange. RADIUS runs over IPv4 in 6rd scenarios, and its known weaknesses are discussed in RFC 2607, RFC 2865 and RFC 2869. IPsec for RADIUS over IPv6 is covered in RFC 3162.

A malicious user could try to obtain unauthorized 6rd configuration through MAC address spoofing or a dictionary attack on the shared 6rd password. Those issues are treated in Section 12 of RFC 5969, and generic DHCP security mechanisms can protect the CE-to-BNG leg.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could pretend to be another customer's router or guess the shared password. The network is private, which lowers the risk.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned one new RADIUS Attribute Type in the Radius Types registry: IPv6-6rd-Configuration, value 173. That is the only registry action in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute got its own official number, 173, so everyone uses the same one.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Whole attribute in octets: 28 + n*6, n being the number of BR addresses.

fields.name: IPv4MaskLen
fields.desc: Count of high-order bits shared by all CE IPv4 addresses; 0 to 32.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: All zero; ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: 6rdPrefixLen
fields.desc: Prefix length in bits; 128 or less.

fields.name: 6rdPrefix
fields.desc: The provider's 6rd IPv6 prefix as a 16-octet address.

fields.name: 6rdBRIPv4Address
fields.desc: A Border Relay IPv4 address; repeated for each relay.
